scope.start: 10b: the challenge to Abba Kohen Bardela from the *get* baraita (11a opens mid-answer)
scope.end: 11b: Rav Ashi's distinction between a gift and a *get*, continuing on 12a

sections.title: Chatzer Mishum Yad: A Get, a Girl's Find, or a Boy's?
sections.gist: The *get* baraita shows that a *chatzer* works as a *yad*, so the Gemara reframes the dispute of R. Yannai and Abba Kohen Bardela three ways: *get* vs. found item, girl vs. boy, or no dispute at all.

bullets.text: The question under the whole passage: is a *chatzer* an extension of the person (*yad*) or his agent (*shaliach*)? If it is *yad*, it should work for minors as their own hand does. Minors cannot appoint agents.
The question of whether *chatzer* is *yad* or *shaliach* runs through the rest of the daf and the next Mishnah's discussion.

chart.caption: Three ways to read the dispute of R. Yannai and Abba Kohen Bardela
rows: A *chatzer* acts as her *yad* for a *get*
Is a found item in her *chatzer* learned from *get*? R. Yannai: yes; Abba Kohen Bardela: no
A *ketanah* acquires a found item in her *chatzer*
Is a *katan* learned from a *ketanah*? R. Yannai: yes; Abba Kohen Bardela: no
None: one statement concerns a girl's *get*, the other a minor's found item

children.title: 'Ve'natan': A Get on Her Roof, Chatzer or Karpef
children.gist: A baraita derives from "*ve'natan*" that a *get* placed on her roof, in her *chatzer* or in her *karpef* divorces her, so how can anyone deny that a *chatzer* works as a *yad*?

bullets.text: The Gemara challenges Abba Kohen Bardela's position as it was explained: does anyone really deny that a *chatzer* is included because it acts as her *yad*?

Baraita on Devarim 24:1: "*ve'natan be'yadah*" alone would teach only her hand. From where do we know her roof, her *chatzer* or her *karpef*? "*Ve'natan*": she is divorced in any case. So a *chatzer* serves as an extension of her hand.
Rashi: the verb comes before its object, and this extends the giving beyond the literal hand.
Tosafot: a *ketanah* too can receive a *get*, and the verse grounds her *chatzer* in her *yad*. So a minor girl's *chatzer* works as *yad*, not as *shaliach*.

children.title: First Answer: Does a Found Item Follow the Get?
children.gist: All agree that a *chatzer* acts as her *yad* for a *get*. R. Yannai learns found items from this and Abba Kohen Bardela does not.

bullets.text: For a *get*, everyone agrees that the *chatzer* is included because it acts as her *yad*.
They disagree about a found item (*metziah*) in her *chatzer*. R. Yannai derives *metziah* from *get*; Abba Kohen Bardela does not.

Why the two might differ: a *get* may need only to be placed on her, not acquired by her, and a *chatzer* counts as "on her person." A *metziah* needs a real *kinyan*, and being in her domain may not supply one.
So the *get* ruling proves that a *chatzer* is *yad* for placement. It leaves open whether, for acquisitions, it is *yad* or *shaliach*.

children.title: Second Answer: A Ketanah's Chatzer vs. a Katan's
children.gist: Alternatively, all agree that a minor girl acquires a found item in her *chatzer*. The dispute is whether a minor boy is learned from her.

bullets.text: For a *ketanah*, everyone derives *metziah* from *get*: she acquires an ownerless item found in her *chatzer*.

R. Yannai derives a *katan* from a *ketanah*, since the laws of acquisition should not differ between them. Abba Kohen Bardela does not: only a girl acquires through her *chatzer*, because the Torah included it for a *get*.
A boy has no *get* for the verse to work through. The only way to treat his *chatzer* as *yad* is by analogy to the girl.

children.title: Third Answer: No Dispute, Two Different Statements
children.gist: Perhaps each Sage spoke of a different case: a girl divorced by a *get* in her *chatzer*, and minors who do not acquire a found item there.

bullets.text: There is no dispute. One statement was that a *ketanah* is divorced by a *get* placed in her *chatzer*. The other was that a minor boy or girl does not acquire an item found in his or her *chatzer*.
This is surprising. Once the Torah shows that a *chatzer* can act as *yad*, why should that hold for a *get* and not for a find? The answer must lie in what *yad* means in each context.

Tosafot: a minor cannot acquire a *metziah* by Torah law, because he lacks *da'at*. If an adult actively places an item in a minor's *chatzer* to give it to him, *da'at acheret* may make it work even for a *katan*.

sections.title: 'Zakhtah Li Sadi': Crippled Deer and Fledglings vs. Runners and Flyers
sections.gist: A field acquires an ownerless animal that others are chasing only if the animal cannot escape: a deer with a broken leg or pigeons that cannot yet fly, not a running deer or flying birds.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one saw people running after a found animal, such as a deer with a broken leg or young pigeons (*gozalot*) that cannot yet fly. He said "*zakhtah li sadi*" (my field has acquired it for me), and his field acquires it for him.
If the deer was running normally or the pigeons were flying, his declaration is nothing: a *chatzer* cannot acquire what will not stay in it.
The Mishnah draws its line at containment: *kinyan chatzer* works only on what the field can actually hold.
The others were chasing it first, yet the first valid *kinyan* is his, made through his field.

sections.title: Omed Be'tzad Sadehu: Standing by an Unsecured Field
sections.gist: Shmuel requires the owner to stand beside his field. The Gemara explains this as the rule for an unsecured *chatzer*, proves it from *shikhchah*, and cites Ulla and Rabba bar bar Chana in agreement.

children.title: Why Stand There? Chatzer Ha'mishtameret vs. an Open Field
children.gist: Shmuel's condition seems to clash with R. Yosei b. R. Chanina's rule that a *chatzer* acquires even without its owner's knowledge. The answer: that rule is for a secured *chatzer*, and an open field acquires only while its owner stands by it.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name: the Mishnah's acquisition works only when the owner is *omed be'tzad sadehu*, standing next to his field.

At first this looks like the same axis as the Mishnah. The broken leg keeps the animal from escaping by itself, and the owner's presence keeps it from getting away. Together they make the field hold it.
Difficulty: R. Yosei b. R. Chanina says that a person's *chatzer* acquires for him even without his knowledge.
Tosafot likewise: the Mishnah's declaration "*zakhtah li sadi*" is *lav davka*, not required. The field would acquire without it.
Answer: that rule concerns a *chatzer ha'mishtameret*, where items stay put unattended. A *chatzer she'einah mishtameret* acquires only if the owner is standing beside it.
A field is the typical unsecured domain: open land with no fence. The owner's presence does for it what a wall does for a yard.

chart.caption: When a *chatzer* acquires an ownerless item

illustration.caption: R. Yosei b. R. Chanina's rule and Shmuel's condition side by side (11a): a secured courtyard acquires even in the owner's absence, while an open field acquires only while he stands beside it.

children.title: The Source: Shikhchah, the Owner in the Field or in Town
children.gist: A baraita on the forgotten sheaf, once untangled, shows that a field acquires a sheaf for its owner only while he stands there. The Gemara then defends this reading against the alternative that the rule is a Torah edict.

children.title: The Owner in Town Who 'Remembers': A Baraita at Odds with Itself
children.gist: The baraita asks whether a sheaf the owner remembered from town and later forgot is *shikhchah*, then derives "in the field, not in the town," and seems to answer both ways.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that an unsecured *chatzer* acquires only while its owner stands beside it.
Baraita: an owner standing in town says, "I know my laborers forgot a sheaf, but since I remember it, it shall not be *shikhchah*." Then he himself forgot it. One might think it is not *shikhchah*.
The verse (Devarim 24:19) says "and you forget a sheaf in the field": in the field, and not in the town.
The difficulty: "one might think it is not *shikhchah*" implies that it is. "In the field, not in the town" implies that a sheaf forgotten from town is not.

children.title: Forgotten at the Outset vs. Remembered, Then Forgotten
children.gist: In the field, a sheaf remembered and then forgotten is not *shikhchah*, because his field acquires it for him while he stands there. From town, even a remembered sheaf becomes *shikhchah*.

bullets.text: The owner in the field: a sheaf forgotten from the outset is *shikhchah*. One he remembered and later forgot is not.
The reason: since he stands beside it, his field is like his *chatzer*, and it acquires the sheaf for him once he remembers it.

The owner in town: even a sheaf remembered and then forgotten is *shikhchah*, because he is not beside it for his *chatzer* to acquire it. So an item in a person's *chatzer* is acquired only if he stands next to it.
A more intuitive reason would be supervision: while the owner is present and aware, the gathering has not been abandoned. The Gemara frames it as possession instead.
The field cannot acquire the sheaf after it has become *shikhchah*, since by then it belongs to the poor. His standing there must mean he never lost hold of it.
The formal rule has sharp edges. Suppose he steps twenty feet away to a neighbor's door just as the laborers forget. The sheaf is *shikhchah*, though he remembers it and will be back in a moment.

children.title: Torah Edict or Kinyan Chatzer? 'Lo Tashuv' and 'Yihyeh'
children.gist: Perhaps the field/town distinction is only a Torah edict. The Gemara shows that the Torah includes sheaves forgotten from town, first from "*lo tashuv*" and, when that phrase is needed elsewhere, from Rav Ashi's "*yihyeh*."

bullets.text: Rejection: perhaps it is a *gezeirat ha'katuv*. In the field it is *shikhchah* and in town it is not, with no connection to acquisition.

Reply: "*lo tashuv lekachto*" (you shall not go back to take it) includes sheaves forgotten from town. So town and field do not differ in principle, and the difference must come from *kinyan chatzer*.
Objection: the phrase is needed to prohibit taking the forgotten sheaf. Reply: then the verse should say "do not take it"; "go back" is extra.
Objection: "*lo tashuv*" is needed for Pe'ah 7:4. A sheaf still ahead of the harvester is not *shikhchah*, one already behind him is, and the rule is whatever falls under "do not go back."
Rav Ashi: the inclusion comes from "*yihyeh*" (it shall be). So the first reading stands: the difference rests on the owner standing beside his *chatzer*, as Shmuel said.

children.title: Ulla and Rabba bar bar Chana: The Same Condition
children.gist: Two more amora'im also require the owner to stand beside his field.

bullets.text: Ulla says the Mishnah's acquisition works only when he is *omed be'tzad sadehu*, and Rabba bar bar Chana says so too.
So the requirement is not Shmuel's alone but widely held.

sections.title: Rabban Gamliel's Tithes at Sea: Chatzer, Agav or Da'at Acheret?
sections.gist: R. Abba challenges Ulla from tithes transferred through rented land far away. The Gemara answers with *kinyan agav*, defended against Rava's *tovat hana'ah* objection, and with Rav Pappa's *da'at acheret*, which Rav Shimi tests against a *get*.

chart.caption: How Rabban Gamliel's tithes passed, and what that means for Ulla's rule
rows: Through the rented place, as their *chatzer*
The recipients were on the ship, not beside the field
*Kinyan agav*: movables along with the rented land
*Tovat hana'ah* is not property: neither *chalifin* nor land can transfer it
Tithes must be given; *chalifin* is a sale, *agav* is a form of giving
*Da'at acheret makneh*: a transfer from a giver needs less

children.title: The Incident on the Ship, and Ulla's Brush-Off
children.gist: Rabban Gamliel gave tithes still in his fields to R. Yehoshua and R. Akiva by renting them the place, though none of them stood by the field. Ulla dismissed the question.

bullets.text: Ma'aser Sheni 5:9: Rabban Gamliel and the Elders were traveling on a ship. He said: the tenth I will measure out is given to Yehoshua ben Chananya, a Levi, and its place is rented to him.
The other tenth, the *ma'aser ani*, is given to Akiva ben Yosef to acquire for the poor, and its place is rented to him.

Rashi: he had left home without tithing and wanted to keep his household from eating *tevel*, so he separated the tithes from afar. Tosafot: "which I will measure out" does not sound like separating now. The tithes had already been separated and had to be given away, at the end-of-three-years deadline.
R. Abba: were R. Yehoshua and R. Akiva standing next to Rabban Gamliel's field? They were all on the ship. So a *chatzer* acquires without its owner standing beside it.
Tosafot presses further: was the place even *mishtameret*? Grain in an open field is not. Even in a house, the household did not know which portion was now theirs and could take it.
Ulla: "This one seems like a Sage who has not studied *halakha*." He dismissed the question without answering it.
